Stage 3 · Grammar

What you have decided, and what you expect

Two future forms, and one question that separates them.

Read these four sentences.
  • Today we are going to visit the floating islands.
  • I’m sure the water will be quite calm.
  • It’s cold, so I’m going to take an extra sweater.
  • Just thought — I’ll take my camera too.
In which sentence did the speaker decide at that exact moment?
English has no future tense. It has several present forms doing future work.

There is no future ending on an English verb. Instead, English uses modals and present forms to talk about what is ahead, and the one you pick tells your listener something about where that future came from — whether it is a prediction, a plan, an arrangement or a timetable.

Will presents the future as decided or predicted at the moment of speaking. That covers opinions about the future (I think more people will live on the water), decisions taken as you speak (That looks heavy — I’ll carry it), offers, promises, refusals, and facts nobody controls (She’ll be thirty next month). Be going to presents the future as already in place: either an intention you formed earlier (We’re going to sell the flat) or a prediction based on evidence you can point at right now (Look at those clouds — it’s going to rain).

Two present forms also do future work. The present continuous expresses a fixed arrangement, usually with another person and usually with a time: We’re seeing the estate agent on Thursday. The present simple expresses a timetable that is fixed by an institution rather than by you: The ferry leaves at seven.

Neither will nor going to is ‘more correct’, and many sentences allow both with a small shift of meaning. But the difference is real and listeners hear it. I’ll have the fish suggests you are choosing at that moment; I’m going to have the fish suggests you decided when you read the menu.

Before you look at the table: the table below arranges the forms by the source of the future — decided now, decided before, arranged with somebody, or fixed by a timetable. That column is the one to read first.
The two forms, side by side
 be going towill

Ask one question. Did you decide before you opened your mouth? Then going to. Did you decide while you were speaking? Then will. That single test covers most of the decisions you will make.

For predictions the question is different. Can you point at the evidence? Look at the sky — it’s going to rain. Or is it your own belief? I think it will rain tomorrow.

The mistake to avoid. Do not use will for a plan you made yesterday: not Tomorrow I will visit my aunt — I bought the ticket last week, but I’m going to visit my aunt.

Offers, promises and refusals always take will. I’ll help you. I won’t tell anybody. The door won’t open. None of these was planned in advance.

Full grammar reference — future forms — will and be going to

What it is

English has no future tense in the way it has a past tense: there is no future ending on the verb. Instead it uses present forms and modals to talk about what is ahead. The two central options at this level are will + base verb and be going to + base verb. Both refer to future time; they differ in what the speaker is signalling about that future.

What it means, and what it does

The choice is about where the future comes from. Will presents the future as something decided or predicted at the moment of speaking — an opinion, an offer, a promise, a decision just taken. Be going to presents it as something already in place: a plan made earlier, or a prediction based on evidence you can point to now. I’ll help you is a decision made as you speak; I’m going to help you means you had already decided.

When and why we use it

There is no future ending on an English verb. Instead, English uses modals and present forms to talk about what is ahead, and the one you pick tells your listener something about where that future came from — whether it is a prediction, a plan, an arrangement or a timetable.

Will presents the future as decided or predicted at the moment of speaking. That covers opinions about the future (I think more people will live on the water), decisions taken as you speak (That looks heavy — I’ll carry it), offers, promises, refusals, and facts nobody controls (She’ll be thirty next month). Be going to presents the future as already in place: either an intention you formed earlier (We’re going to sell the flat) or a prediction based on evidence you can point at right now (Look at those clouds — it’s going to rain).

Two present forms also do future work. The present continuous expresses a fixed arrangement, usually with another person and usually with a time: We’re seeing the estate agent on Thursday. The present simple expresses a timetable that is fixed by an institution rather than by you: The ferry leaves at seven.

Neither will nor going to is ‘more correct’, and many sentences allow both with a small shift of meaning. But the difference is real and listeners hear it. I’ll have the fish suggests you are choosing at that moment; I’m going to have the fish suggests you decided when you read the menu.

Typical situations

You need these forms for making predictions, announcing plans and intentions, offering help, making promises, arranging to meet somebody, and talking about schedules and timetables.

  • Predictions and opinions about the future — often with I think, I’m sure, probably, I expect.I think more people will live on the water in fifty years.
  • Decisions made at the moment of speaking — the speaker decides as they speak; offers and promises work the same way.That looks heavy — I’ll carry it for you.
  • Intentions and plans decided earlier — be going to, whether or not the arrangements are made.We’re going to sell the flat and move onto a boat.
  • Predictions with present evidence — you can see the reason for the prediction right now.Look at those clouds — it’s going to rain.
  • Fixed arrangements with other people — the present continuous, when a time and place are already agreed.We’re seeing the estate agent on Thursday.
  • Timetables and schedules — the present simple, for fixed public timetables.The ferry leaves at seven every morning.
  • Future facts you cannot control — will, because there is no plan behind them.She’ll be thirty next month.

How it differs from similar structures

will = decided now, or a prediction from opinion · be going to = decided before now, or a prediction from evidence you can see. I’ll have the fish (choosing now) vs I’m going to have the fish (I decided when I read the menu).
be going to = my intention · present continuous = an arrangement already fixed with somebody else, usually with a time. I’m going to visit her vs I’m visiting her on Sunday.

How to build it

will: subject + will + base verb  (’ll in speech)
be going to: subject + am / is / are + going to + base verb
present continuous (arrangement): subject + am / is / are + verb-ing + time expression
present simple (timetable): subject + base verb (+ -s) + time expression
will — affirmativeI will go · I’ll go — the same for every person.
will — negativeI will not go · I won’t go
will — questionWill you go? · What will you do?
going to — affirmativeI’m going to move · she’s going to move · they’re going to move
going to — negativeI’m not going to move · he isn’t going to move
going to — questionAre you going to move? · What are you going to do?
Short answersYes, I will. / No, I won’t. / Yes, I am. / No, she isn’t.
With probablyprobably goes after will but before won’t: I’ll probably go · I probably won’t go.

Saying it — contractions and stress

  • will is almost always contracted to ’ll after a pronoun and is barely audible: I’ll, we’ll, they’ll. The full will sounds emphatic or formal.
  • won’t /wəʊnt/ must be clearly distinguished from want /wɒnt/ — the vowel is the difference.
  • In relaxed speech going to before a verb reduces to gonna /ˈɡʌnə/. Recognise it when listening, but write going to.

Usage notes and exceptions

  • Neither form is ‘more correct’. Many sentences allow both with a small shift in meaning, and native speakers move between them constantly.
  • For a plan you have already made, be going to and the present continuous are often both possible. The continuous suggests the arrangement is fixed with someone else: I’m going to see the doctor (my intention) vs I’m seeing the doctor at four (appointment booked).
  • Avoid going to go where you can — I’m going to the coast is more natural than I’m going to go to the coast.
  • After if, when, as soon as, until, before, after, use a present form, not will: I’ll call you when I arrive. This is the same rule as Lesson 5.
  • Shall survives mainly in offers and suggestions with I and we: Shall I open the window? It is not a general future form in modern English.
  • Will is also used for instant reactions, refusals and promises: I’ll get it, The door won’t open, I promise I won’t forget.

Watch out — the mistakes learners really make

  • I will move to a houseboat next year — I decided last month. → I’m going to move to a houseboat next year.A decision made earlier takes be going to.
  • Look at the sky, it will rain. → Look at the sky, it’s going to rain.There is visible evidence now, so be going to is required.
  • I’ll to call you tomorrow. → I’ll call you tomorrow.Will is a modal and takes the base verb with no to.
  • When I will arrive, I’ll text you. → When I arrive, I’ll text you.No will after a time conjunction.
  • She will probably not come. → She probably won’t come.Probably goes before a negative auxiliary.
  • Are you go to sell the flat? → Are you going to sell the flat?Be going to keeps going and to.

More examples in context

  • predictionI think artificial islands will become normal within twenty years.
  • instant decisionThere’s no ferry until six — I’ll walk.
  • offerYou look exhausted. I’ll make room for one more.
  • promiseDon’t worry, I won’t tell anyone.
  • prior intentionWe’re going to get rid of half our books before we move.
  • evidence-based predictionThe water’s rising fast — those houses are going to flood.
  • arrangementWe’re meeting the architect at ten on Friday.
  • timetableThe last ferry leaves at half past eleven.
  • hedged predictionCities will probably keep growing inland first.
  • negative predictionMost people probably won’t want to live miles from anywhere.

A tip for remembering it

Before you choose, ask: did I decide this before I started speaking? If yes → going to. If I am deciding right now → will. For predictions ask a second question: can I point at the evidence? If yes → going to. If it is just my opinion → will.

Before you practise — the key rules

  1. Will + base verb; be going to + base verb. Neither takes to after will.
  2. Will = decision made now, opinion, offer, promise, unavoidable fact.
  3. Be going to = intention decided earlier, or prediction with visible evidence.
  4. Present continuous = a fixed arrangement; present simple = a timetable.
  5. Probably comes after will but before won’t.
  6. Never use will after if, when, as soon as, until, before, after.

Stage 5 · Main input

Living on the water

A family whose home floats, and what they think happens next.

Before you read: in several countries, people are building permanent homes on water.

Why do you think they do it?

Choose one. The text gives more than one reason — see how many you find.

Living on the water

Around the world, people are moving off the land — not because they want an adventure, but because the land is running out.

AOn Lake Titicaca, high in the Andes, there are islands you can pull apart with your hands. The Uros people build them from reeds, layer on layer, and add fresh reeds on top every few weeks as the bottom rots away. A well-kept island will last about thirty years. There are no cliffs, no rocks and no valleys here — just a flat green landscape that moves slightly underfoot, and about two thousand inhabitants who have lived this way for centuries.

BFour thousand miles away, in Amsterdam, a very different community is doing something similar for very modern reasons. The city has run out of space. Prices in the suburbs are impossible, and moving inland is not an option, so about a hundred households have settled down on the water instead. Their homes are permanent and connected to the city like any other: post, internet, solar power on the roof.

CMarijke has lived on one of them for six years. “People think we are going to feel cramped, packed in like sardines,” she says. “Come and look.” Inside, the rooms are ordinary; there is a communal garden shared by the whole block and a thirty-minute ferry service to the mainland. “The one thing you learn is to make room. Everything you own has to earn its place. I’ll never go back to a house with an attic full of things I have forgotten about.”

DNot everybody is convinced. Building on water is expensive, and critics argue that the money will always go where the profit is. In the Maldives, a company is developing artificial islands to provide housing for the country’s poorer citizens, and by 2030 it expects twenty thousand people to be living there. Others say the same technology will end up producing luxury housing for people who could live anywhere they liked.

EWhat is certain is that the pressure is not going to disappear. By 2050, roughly two thirds of the world’s population will live in cities, and a large number of the biggest ones sit on a coast or a river. Some of them will build upwards. Some will build outwards, into the suburbs. A few, planners think, will build onto the water — not as an experiment, but because there will be nowhere else to put people.

FMarijke is more modest about it. She did not set off six years ago to solve a global problem; she wanted a home she could afford within reach of her work. “I don’t think everyone is going to live like this,” she says. “But you get used to it very fast. After about a month, you stop noticing that the floor is moving. And then it is just where you live.”

Written for this course. Details of the Uros islands, the Amsterdam floating districts and the Maldives project are drawn from published municipal planning documents and UNESCO reporting.
